Consult Summary:
- 26-year-old woman with 3-day history of progressively worsening right-predominant periorbital/diffuse headache (8/10) with photophobia, transient flashing lights at onset, nausea (no vomiting) — working diagnosis: probable acute migraine; plan: stronger analgesia prescription, headache diary, eye check, and follow-up in 1–2 weeks.

History:
- Presenting complaint and timeline:
  - Headache began ~3 days ago, gradual onset while at work, worse by next morning and progressively worse overall.
  - Location: diffuse but mainly around right eye/periorbital.
  - Character: mostly dull with intermittent sharper episodes; constant with fluctuating severity.
  - Severity: reported 8/10.
- Associated symptoms / review of systems:
  - Photophobia — "light is quite annoying, my eyes... it hurts to look at bright lights."
  - Transient visual phenomenon at onset described as "weird shooting lights."
  - Nausea / feeling sick; no vomiting.
  - Difficulty focusing; reduced work ability.
  - No neck stiffness, no fever, no rash, no focal neurological deficits (no weakness, no speech difficulty), no recent head injury.
- Pertinent negatives:
  - No vomiting, no vision loss, no neck pain/stiffness, no fever, no rash, no recent trauma.
- Past medical history, allergies, medications:
  - Reports otherwise fit and well; no chronic medical conditions specified.
  - No regular medications.
  - Recent OTC ibuprofen taken ~3 tablets per day for the last 2 days with minimal benefit.
  - No known drug allergies.
- Social / preventive health:
  - Works in IT with prolonged computer/screen use.
  - Wears glasses since childhood; no recent eye test.
  - Lives with housemates.
  - Social smoker and drinks alcohol socially.
  - Family history: mother and sister have frequent migraines.
  - Contraceptive/pregnancy status not clearly documented.

Examination:
- Vitals: none recorded in transcript.
- Observed / reported exam findings:
  - No focal neurological deficits reported on history.
  - No neck stiffness on review.
  - No fever or rash reported.
  - Visual symptoms described by patient (photophobia, transient flashing lights); no objective vision loss reported.
- No formal neurological, ENT, or ocular exam documented in transcript.

Impression:
- Working clinical impression:
  - Probable acute migraine (most likely).
    - Support: unilateral-predominant periorbital pain, photophobia, transient visual phenomena ("shooting lights"), nausea, poor response to OTC ibuprofen, positive family history of migraine, age and sex typical for migraine.
  - Secondary considerations (top alternatives from DDx consistent with transcript):
    1. Tension-type headache / stress-related or cervicogenic headache (medium likelihood) — supports: dull, diffuse pain, relation to prolonged screen use and work stress; opposes: prominent photophobia/visual symptoms and nausea which favor migraine.
    2. Eyestrain / uncorrected refractive error / computer vision syndrome (medium–low likelihood) — supports: prolonged screen use, no recent eye test, improvement with reduced screen brightness; opposes: flashing lights/photophobia and nausea pointing more to migraine.
  - Less likely causes per DDx (not supported by current history): acute sinusitis, intracranial mass, meningitis/SAH/dissection (no fever, no neck stiffness, no sudden thunderclap onset, no focal deficits).

Plan:
- Acute treatment / prescriptions discussed in visit (as per clinician):
  - Offer prescription for stronger analgesia (clinician offered naproxen as an alternative NSAID).
  - Consider adding paracetamol and/or codeine-containing analgesic if needed (clinician discussed these options).
  - Clinician reviewed ibuprofen dosing and advised appropriate OTC dosing (stated: up to two tablets three times daily).
- Symptom management and self-care:
  - Reduce screen brightness and take breaks from screen work as feasible.
  - Obtain an updated eye examination given longstanding glasses and current visual symptoms.
  - Keep a headache diary to identify triggers and pattern.
- Follow-up / safety netting:
  - Arrange follow-up in 1–2 weeks to reassess; earlier review if headaches become more frequent (discussion of prophylactic therapy if recurrent).
  - Return or seek urgent care sooner for red flags: new/worsening visual loss, focal neurological deficits (weakness, speech changes), severe sudden worsening of headache, persistent vomiting, fever, or any other concerning deterioration.
- Additional recommendations (consistent with DDx and clinician discussion):
  - Monitor analgesic use and avoid frequent repetitive use that could risk medication-overuse headache; if headaches become frequent, discuss prophylactic therapy.
  - If symptoms do not respond to prescribed treatment or worsen, consider further evaluation (neurologic exam, targeted ocular assessment, and imaging if indicated).

Quality checks (document_quality):
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - Vital signs (BP, HR, temperature).
  - Formal neurological and cranial nerve / visual acuity exam documentation.
  - Detailed ocular exam (fundoscopy, visual fields) and recent eye prescription details.
  - Contraceptive and pregnancy status (relevant for medication choices and hormonal migraine consideration).
  - Exact dosing and prescription details (drug names, strengths, durations) not recorded in transcript.
  - Any plan for imaging or laboratory testing (none documented).
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx:
  - None direct; DDx expanded on alternative and serious causes for consideration but did not conflict with transcript facts. (If red-flag features develop, DDx recommendations support escalation.)
- Transcript quality comment:
  - History is generally clear and adequate for initial assessment of headache; audio contains typical conversational fillers but key symptoms and timeline are documented.
  - Lacks objective exam findings and vital signs; some preventive/obstetric details (contraception/pregnancy) are incomplete.
